prompt: In SLSA's threat overview, how are dependencies placed on the chain?

choices.text: As letter Z, after usage
choices.why: There is no letter for them; that is the point of how SLSA treats them.

choices.text: Each one carries the whole chain again, A to H
choices.why: Right. A compromised dependency is one of those letters going wrong one level down.

choices.text: Only at H, the choice of package
choices.why: H covers choosing a package; a dependency can break at any of its own letters.

choices.text: Outside SLSA, which covers only your build
choices.why: SLSA names dependency threats explicitly.

prompt: Match each SLSA letter to the part of linkbox it concerns.

pairs.right: the name and version the cluster asks for

prompt: Why are A, the producer, and I, usage, almost absent from the table of controls?

choices.text: Pipelines cannot check intent, or later configuration
choices.why: Right: one is about whom you trust, the other belongs to runtime and admission.

choices.text: No incident on record has ever happened at either of those letters
choices.why: SLSA lists examples at both; they are just out of a pipeline's reach.

choices.text: They are both covered by signing the artefacts
choices.why: A signature says who published, not whether that person meant well.

choices.text: SLSA gave up on them in its latest version
choices.why: They are in the threat overview; SLSA says it does not address them.

prompt: SolarWinds' compromised Orion builds carried a valid SolarWinds signature. What does that teach about signing?

choices.text: Signatures are broken by now and should be dropped from pipelines
choices.why: They do what they claim; the claim is narrower than people assume.

choices.text: The attackers had stolen the signing key
choices.why: The signing was SolarWinds' own, after an altered build; no stolen key was needed.

choices.text: It says who published, not what the source was
choices.why: Right. Provenance and an independent build answer the second question.

choices.text: Signing should happen before the build
choices.why: There is nothing to sign before the artefact exists.

prompt: How was the modified Codecov Bash Uploader discovered?

choices.text: A malware scanner flagged the script
choices.why: No scanner found it; a person comparing two values did.

choices.text: A customer compared its SHA-256
choices.why: Right, with the one published beside it: exactly the check pip's hash mode does.

choices.text: GitHub's secret scanning saw the leaked tokens
choices.why: The secrets went to an outside server, not to a repository.

choices.text: Codecov's own audit of its storage
choices.why: Codecov learnt of it from a customer.

prompt: In March 2025, which workflows using tj-actions/changed-files kept running the old, safe code?

choices.text: Those that used a major tag such as @v45
choices.why: Those are exactly the tags the attacker moved.

choices.text: Those on private repositories
choices.why: Private repositories ran the same code; their logs were just less exposed.

choices.text: Those pinned to a full commit hash
choices.why: Right: a commit hash names one tree of files and cannot be moved.

choices.text: Those that ran it only on pull requests
choices.why: The trigger did not matter; the code the tag pointed at did.

prompt: Why does SLSA use event-stream as its example of a dependency threat?

choices.text: Its published code was not in its source
choices.why: Right: the malicious code was on npm and not on GitHub, a package that does not match its source.

choices.text: The package had a typo in its name
choices.why: That is typosquatting, letter H; event-stream's name was the real one.

choices.text: npm itself, the registry, was compromised by the attacker
choices.why: The registry worked as designed; the package changed hands legitimately.

choices.text: Its build server was broken into
choices.why: Nothing in the incident involves a build server.

prompt: A project's lockfile pinned ua-parser-js 0.7.28 on the day versions 0.7.29, 0.8.0 and 1.0.0 were published by the stolen account. Which statements are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A fresh install from that lockfile installed 0.7.28
choices.why: Yes: a lock does not take new versions by itself.

choices.text: An automatic update that day could have brought in a malicious version
choices.why: Yes, which is why a cooling-off period matters.

choices.text: The lockfile made the project immune to every future compromise of the package
choices.why: It protects the pinned version until somebody updates it, and no further.

choices.text: Two-factor authentication on the maintainer's account would have helped
choices.why: Yes: the account takeover was the way in.

prompt: xz's backdoor was activated from the release tarball and was not in the Git repository. Which control is aimed at exactly that gap?

choices.text: Pinning xz by version in every image
choices.why: The malicious versions were real releases; a pin would have pinned them.

choices.text: Building from the repository
choices.why: Right, or comparing the tarball with it: the difference was exactly where the trigger was.

choices.text: Scanning the tarball with an image scanner
choices.why: No advisory existed before the disclosure, so a scanner had nothing to match.

choices.text: Signing the tarball with the maintainer's key
choices.why: The tarball was published by a maintainer; a signature would have been valid.

prompt: Put the four dependency incidents in the order they happened.
pip refused the wheel from the local mirror with `Expected` and `Got`. What did `Got` contain?

choices.text: The hash from the requirements file
choices.why: That is `Expected`, the value you pinned.

choices.text: The hash PyPI publishes for blinker 1.9.0
choices.why: pip never asked PyPI; the file came from the local index.

choices.text: The SHA-256 of the file that actually arrived
choices.why: Right: the wheel with one byte added, so a different hash.

choices.text: The hash of the previous version of blinker
choices.why: No other version was involved; same name, same version, different bytes.

prompt: Your lock has a hash for every file, and a maintainer's stolen account publishes a malicious release. In which case does your hash fail to protect you?

choices.text: When the lock is updated to it before anybody looked
choices.why: Right: the hash then faithfully pins the malicious file. A cooling-off period is the defence.

choices.text: When the release is installed from a mirror
choices.why: A mirror serving different bytes is refused; that is what the hash is for.

choices.text: When the package publishes more than one wheel per release
choices.why: A lock lists a hash per file; pip accepts any listed one.

choices.text: When pip runs outside of any virtual environment at all
choices.why: Where pip installs does not change what it verifies.

prompt: pip's ___ mode installs a file only if its SHA-256 is one the requirements file lists.
Where did the hash in the scratch requirements file come from, and why does the lesson say that step deserves care?

choices.text: From the PyPI web page, which somebody could have spoofed
choices.why: It came from `pip hash` on your own download.

choices.text: Your own download, which could itself be tampered
choices.why: Right: `pip hash` on it, and a tampered download would pin the tampered file. That is why lesson 15 takes hashes from the index's records, on a date.

choices.text: From the wheel's own RECORD file, which lists it
choices.why: RECORD lists the hashes of the files inside the wheel, not of the wheel.

choices.text: From uv's cache, which only keeps verified files
choices.why: uv played no part in that step.

prompt: With `--extra-index-url` pointing at your index (packaging 0.1) beside PyPI, which version of packaging did pip download? Give the number.
Given the same two indexes, why did uv install packaging 0.1 by default?

choices.text: uv reads only the indexes served from localhost, by design
choices.why: uv reads any index; it chose by order, not by address.

choices.text: First index with the name wins, and the extra one is first
choices.why: Right. `unsafe-best-match` restores pip's highest-version rule.

choices.text: 0.1 was in uv's cache
choices.why: Caching does not choose between versions.

choices.text: uv prefers the lowest version it finds, to be on the safe side
choices.why: It did not compare versions across indexes at all.

prompt: Your company registers placeholders on PyPI for its twelve internal package names. A thirteenth internal package is added next month. What does the placeholder strategy do for it?

choices.text: It protects it, because the company's namespace is now reserved
choices.why: PyPI has no company namespaces; each name is claimed one by one.

choices.text: Nothing, until somebody remembers to claim that name too
choices.why: Right: placeholders close the door for those names and no others, which is why one index comes first.

choices.text: It makes pip prefer the internal index for every name
choices.why: pip's rule does not change; it still takes the highest version from the pool.

choices.text: It blocks typosquatting of the twelve names as well
choices.why: A typo of a name is a different name, which nobody claimed.

prompt: What is typosquatting, as SLSA places it?

choices.text: A name one keystroke from a popular one, at H
choices.why: Right. It needs a person to type a name wrong once.

choices.text: A stolen publishing account, at F, the publication
choices.why: That is ua-parser-js's case, a different way in.

choices.text: A moved Git tag, inside the build
choices.why: That is tj-actions.

choices.text: A backdoor hidden inside a release tarball, at letter D
choices.why: That is xz.

prompt: Match each incident to the control that would have caught it.

pairs.right: check the hash before running the script

prompt: A team's installers use `--extra-index-url` for the company index, and every requirement is pinned with a hash. Somebody registers one of the internal names on PyPI with version 99. What happens on the next install?

choices.text: pip installs version 99 from PyPI, the higher one
choices.why: The pin and its hash name the internal version; a different file is refused.

choices.text: pip installs the pinned internal version
choices.why: Right, because its hash matches: the hash covers what the index arrangement does not. One index would be better still.

choices.text: pip asks the user which index to trust
choices.why: pip never asks; it decides by its rule.

choices.text: The install fails because two indexes have the name
choices.why: Having the name on two indexes is normal; pip does not fail on it.

prompt: Which single idea does the lesson say most of the controls share?

choices.text: Scan everything twice
choices.why: Scanning finds known flaws; none of the seven was known in advance.

choices.text: Trust only signed software
choices.why: SolarWinds was signed.

choices.text: Compare what arrived with a record of what was meant
choices.why: Right: a hash, a commit, provenance, a lockfile diff.

choices.text: Use fewer dependencies
choices.why: Fewer helps, but several incidents were in the build, not in a dependency.
